At that time, the entire great assembly was filled with doubt and they said to one another:
"The four fearlessnesses and the eighteen unique qualities... [From the point] "At that time, the entire great assembly was filled with doubt" onwards.
The fifth section of questions within the temporal framework of the discourse on the sutra.
This section contains four distinct parts:
first, the collective doubt of the great assembly;
"Each said to one another" and so forth constitutes the second section, the discourse on their deliberations;
"Previously [the Buddha] has already acted for our sake" and so forth constitutes the third section, which introduces the matter of their doubt;
and "At that time, the sixteen great kings" and so forth constitutes the fourth section, clarifying that the Tathāgata’s affairs are unknowable.
The initial text states "all [said] so" (僉然), meaning that everyone agreed.
The second section, the "Discourse on Distinguishing," refers to those who spoke to one another, which signifies mutual consultation.
Regarding the four fearlessnesses (四無畏): wishing to resolve their doubts, he first cites the Buddha’s virtues; therefore, he clarifies the four fearlessnesses.
First, omniscience; second, the destruction of outflows; third, the path to the cessation of suffering; and fourth, the teaching on the obstacles to the path.
Regarding their common designation as "fearlessness," the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā* states: "Because one does not fear external challenges, it is called fearlessness."

The eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*) are: first, no failure in bodily action; second, no failure in verbal action; third, no failure in mindfulness; fourth, absence of divergent thoughts; fifth, absence of an unconcentrated mind; sixth, absence of a mind that relinquishes without full awareness; seventh, no decrease in great desire; eighth, no decrease in diligence; ninth, no decrease in mindfulness; tenth, no decrease in wisdom; eleventh, no decrease in liberation; twelfth, no decrease in the knowledge and vision of liberation; thirteenth, bodily action follows the movement of wisdom; fourteenth, verbal action follows the movement of wisdom; fifteenth, mental action follows the movement of wisdom; sixteenth, unimpeded wisdom knows the past; seventeenth, unimpeded wisdom knows the future; eighteenth, unimpeded wisdom knows the present.

“O World-Honored One of Great Enlightenment, the Dharmakāya endowed with the five eyes, you have previously, for the sake of us and this great assembly, expounded over twenty-nine years the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*, the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā*, the *Rājapraśnīya-prajñāpāramitā*, and the *Prabhāsa-prajñāpāramitā*. Today, the Tathāgata emits a great radiance; what purpose does this serve?”
Regarding the five eyes: the single eye of the Tathāgata is the ultimate realization of all paths; why, then, would these five be necessary?
Because the objects are themselves wisdom, there are these five.
The fleshly eye, having illuminated the vajra, returns to the exhaustion of all dharmas.
The divine eye illuminates the ultimate truth of the Tathāgata’s fruition; this is termed "beyond obstructions."
The wisdom-eye (prajñā-cakṣus) illuminates the emptiness of all phenomena, such as the constant and the impermanent.
The dharma-eye (dharma-cakṣus) illuminates the causes, effects, principles, and phenomena of all conditioned dharmas.
The Buddha-eye (buddha-cakṣus) is the ultimate realization of all paths.
The Dharma-body (dharmakāya) takes the true Dharma as its essence and wondrous understanding as its substance; hence it is called the Dharma-body.
Great Enlightenment (mahābodhi) is the ultimate among all forms of awakening; thus it is named Great Enlightenment.
"Bhagavān" (World-Honored One): In foreign lands it is called *Lokanātha*, which here is translated as "World-Honored One.
*Loka* means "world," and *nātha* means "honored one.
Previously, for our sake, he has already provided the third introductory section concerning matters of doubt.
In the twenty-ninth year, the four Prajñās have already been explained; now, on the eighth day of the first month of the thirtieth year, he again emits light—how does this differ from what preceded?

At Rājagṛha on Vulture Peak, he preached the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*; at Śrāvastī, he preached the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā* and the *Devaparipṛcchā-prajñāpāramitā*. Later, returning to Rājagṛha on Vulture Peak, he preached the *Prabhāsa-prajñāpāramitā* and the *Aṣṭasāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā*, providing a complete account of the *Prabhāsa-prajñāpāramitā*.
"Today the Tathāgata has emitted a great radiance; what purpose does this serve?
This is a statement expressing doubt and indecision.
According to the *Vajrasamādhi-śāstra*, the eight divisions of the *Prajñāpāramitā* are elucidated, whereas this sutra elucidates the five divisions.

At that time, among the sixteen great kings, the ruler of Śrāvastī, King Prasenajit, was named Candraprabha (Moonlight). His virtuous conduct encompassed the ten stages (*bhūmi*), the six perfections (*pāramitā*), the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣikadharma*), and the four kinds of indestructible purity (*avetyaprasāda*); he practiced and transformed others through the Mahāyāna.
At that time, among the sixteen great kingdoms, the fourth clarifies that the matters concerning the Tathāgata are unknowable. This section has two parts:

first, the naming of King Prasenajit; second, the explanation of the Buddha’s teaching on the unknowability of the Tathāgata. Regarding the first part: [the text] sets forth the name of King Prasenajit.
Regarding the section on "Virtuous Conduct," this is a praise of his virtues.
First, concerning the explanation of the name, two causes and conditions shall be clarified.

If the name was established based on his parents, it was called Vijaya (Victorious Army). He was born on the same day as the Tathāgata; later, because he was able to defeat powerful enemies through his great prowess and was always victorious in every place where he fought, his parents bestowed upon him the name Vijaya.
"February Light" (Candraprabha) is a title bestowed by the people of the world.
The Buddha is like the sunlight, and King Prasenajit assists the Buddha just as moonlight does; therefore, he is named "Moonlight."
Below the ten stages of spiritual practice (*daśabhūmi*), the next section clarifies the praise of virtues.
As for what are called the "ten stages," they are as explained above.
Regarding the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*): first is *dāna* (generosity), which takes the relinquishing of wealth as its capacity.
Second is ethical discipline (*śīla*), which has the meaning of preventing wrongdoing;
third is patience (*kṣānti*), which takes the cessation of anger as its function;
fourth is diligence (*vīrya*), which takes energetic exertion as its application.
The five dhyānas take the concentration of the mind as their virtue;
the sixth, prajñā, takes the penetrating insight into the absence of intrinsic meaning as its function.
This is explained in detail in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.

Regarding the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment: there are four groups of three, two groups of five, one group of seven, and one group of eight. Although they are named thirty-seven, they take ten fundamental dharmas as their basis—namely, faith, precept, mindfulness, concentration, wisdom, diligence, reflection, equanimity, joy, and relinquishment. Within these ten, six are expanded into sixteen and four are established, thus forming the thirty-seven.
Regarding the opening of the six: faith is divided into two—faith as a faculty (*śraddhendriya*) and faith as a power (*śraddhābala*).
Ethical discipline (*śīla*) is divided into three—right speech (*samyagvāc*), right action (*samyakkarmānta*), and right livelihood (*samyagājīva*).
Mindfulness (*smṛti*) is divided into four—mindfulness as a faculty, mindfulness as a power, the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness (*smṛtisambodhyaṅga*), and right mindfulness (*samyaksmṛti*).
There are eight aspects of diligence: the four right efforts, the faculty of diligence, the power of diligence, the factor of enlightenment of diligence, and right diligence.
There are eight aspects of concentration: the four bases of power, the faculty of concentration, the power of concentration, the factor of enlightenment of concentration, and right concentration.
The eight factors of wisdom are: the four foundations of mindfulness, the faculty of wisdom, the power of wisdom, the factor of enlightenment of investigation of phenomena, and right view.
The four kinds of unshakable confidence are: unshakable confidence in the Buddha, confidence in the Dharma, confidence in the Sangha, and unshakable confidence in the precepts.
Regarding those who practice the transformation of the Mahāyāna, this refers to the Mahāyāna propagated by Candraprabha.

He questioned eight hundred people in succession, including the laymen Ratnacchattra and Dharmaviśuddhanāman; he further questioned five thousand people, including Subhūti and Śāriputra; and he further questioned ten thousand people, including Maitreya and Siṃhanāda, yet none were able to answer.
As for the "successive questioning," it refers to requesting a resolution of one's doubts.
When the ten thousand people, from the householder Ratnacchattra to Siṃhanāda, were unable to answer, the Tathāgata emitted light; they did not know what dharma he intended to proclaim.
This is not something known by those of lower stations; the Tathāgata will surely speak of it himself once he has emerged from meditative absorption, which is why he did not answer.

At that time, King Prasenajit immediately produced eighty thousand kinds of music through his supernormal powers, and the various devas of the eighteen Brahma realms and the six heavens of desire likewise produced eighty thousand kinds of music. Their sounds shook the trichiliocosm, reaching as far as the Buddha-lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges throughout the ten directions where there were beings with whom he shared a karmic connection.
From that Buddha-land in another direction, the Bodhisattva Dharma-Go, together with a great assembly of five hundred million billion beings, came to enter this great gathering;
from the east, the Bodhisattva Jewel-Pillar, together with a great assembly of nine million billion beings, came to enter this great gathering;
from the north, the Bodhisattva Nature-of-Space, together with a great assembly of one hundred thousand million billion beings, came to enter this great gathering.
From the western direction, the Bodhisattva Suvihita arrived at this great assembly together with a multitude as numerous as the sands of ten Ganges Rivers;
the same was true for the other six directions.
They likewise performed music, collectively producing immeasurable musical performances to awaken the Tathāgata.

At that time, King Prasenajit descended, and during the sixth section of the introductory sequence of the sutra, Candraprabha and various devas performed music and praised the Buddha, summoning the assemblies from the ten directions to come and hear the sutra.
Within this, there are three parts:
first, Candraprabha performs eighty thousand kinds of music;
second, from the twenty-eight Brahmās downward, the various devas perform music and praise the Buddha.
Third, "Those from Other Directions" below clarifies the gathering of Bodhisattvas from the ten directions, who perform immeasurable music to awaken the Tathāgata.
Regarding the Bodhisattva Fanguo (Weapon-Spear) of the southern direction, each is distinguished by a title based on a specific virtue.
Even in the second dhyāna, there is still no [distraction], yet one may be moved by the judgment of sound.
What is now called "awakening to the Tathāgata" clarifies that there is a responsive stimulus from sentient beings.
The Buddha, immediately perceiving the time and grasping the faculties of the assembly, arises from samādhi and takes his seat upon a lotus lion-throne, like the King of Vajra Mountains.
The great assembly rejoiced, and each manifested immeasurable supernatural powers, remaining together in the earth and the void.

The Buddha, knowing the time had come, descended and spoke the scripture; this is the seventh section within the introductory sequence of the sutra, clarifying the stage where the Tathāgata arises from samādhi.
"Knowing the time" refers to the time when the Mahāyāna Dharma may be preached.
"Attaining the faculties of sentient beings" means knowing that the capacities of those beings have ripened.

"Arising from meditative concentration" clarifies that the Tathāgata has profoundly and skillfully penetrated dependent origination and skillfully discerned the capacities of beings; he arises because he desires to manifest his great function.

The Tathāgata’s three karmas benefit sentient beings: what was explained above regarding the emission of light and the raining down of flowers illustrates the benefit of sentient beings through bodily karma;
from the "Chapter on Emptiness" (*Śūnyatā-parivarta*) onwards, the uttering of sounds to proclaim the teachings illustrates the benefit of sentient beings through vocal karma.
The physical and verbal [karmas] do not act in isolation; they must be accompanied by mental karma (*manaskarma*).
When mental karma exerts its influence in the unseen, such as causing the earth to tremble and so forth, this is mental karma benefiting sentient beings.
Since he intends to manifest verbal karma, he therefore emerges from meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Regarding "sitting upon a lotus lion-throne": the lotus signifies softness and suppleness, intended to manifest a mark of extraordinary excellence.
As for the "lion-throne," the *Śāstra* states: "It is not an actual lion, nor is it a lion made of wood or stone."
"Because the Tathāgata is the lion among men, whatever place he sits upon—whether a throne or a couch—is called a 'lion-throne. Regarding "the king of diamond mountains":

it is like Mount Sumeru, which rests securely within the great ocean and cannot be moved by the four winds; this illustrates that the Tathāgata’s wisdom rests securely within the emptiness of the *dharmatā* and cannot be moved by the four kinds of heterodox teachers; therefore, it is called the "king of diamond mountains."

Regarding the statement that "the great assembly rejoiced and each manifested immeasurable supernatural powers": previously, seeing the Tathāgata enter meditative absorption and extensively manifest his spiritual powers, they were hesitant and undecided in their minds, and thus did not rejoice.

Now, seeing him emerge from absorption and sit upon the lion throne, about to preach the Dharma, he will resolve their doubts and generate understanding within them; because this profound benefit is so great, it is called "rejoicing."

Regarding the phrase "the ground is where the great assembly dwells in space": those with supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) remain suspended in the air, while those without supernormal powers remain upon the ground.

**Chapter Two: Contemplating Emptiness** *The Benevolent Kings’ Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra for Protecting the State: Chapter Two, Contemplating Emptiness.* From the beginning up to this point, the introductory section (*nidāna*) has been clarified. From here on, the main exposition (*samyag-deśanā*) will be clarified.
The meaning of the introduction having been fully expounded, the primary teaching (zhengzong) should now be revealed; this is for the purpose of clarifying the correct discourse.
Within the text of the primary teaching, although there are six chapters, their meaning may be summarized into four:
first, the first three chapters clarify the capacity to protect *prajñā*, which is also termed "internal protection" (*neihu*).
The second chapter, "Protecting the Nation," explains the nation to be protected, which is also termed "external protection";
the third chapter, "Scattering Flowers," demonstrates the ritual for material offerings and instructs people on how to perform worship;

the fourth chapter, "Receiving and Maintaining," clarifies the virtuous conduct and physical characteristics of those who propagate the sutra, and exhorts future generations to rely upon and study this scripture.
These first three chapters constitute three distinct sections:

the chapter "Contemplating Emptiness" clarifies the protection of the fruit; the chapter "Teaching and Transforming" clarifies the protection of the causes of the ten stages by instructing sentient beings to initiate practice; and the chapter "The Two Truths" discusses and distinguishes the non-duality of the two truths.
The protection of the fruit is not without cause, for it is established to protect the fruit;
within the protection of the cause, the fruit is not absent, for this clarifies that cause.

Within non-discrimination, cause and fruit are primordially pure; they are spoken of as a single path merely for the sake of causes and conditions. Do not harbor a mind of grasping at existence and form fixed attachments.

Regarding what is called "contemplating emptiness": the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, by means of their wondrous wisdom of signlessness, illuminate the wondrous realm of signlessness; as both internal and external merge into stillness, and both conditions and contemplation are quiescent, it is therefore called "contemplating emptiness."
Therefore, the subsequent text states: "To perceive objects and perceive wisdom is not the vision of the noble ones.
Furthermore, it says that "contemplation" refers to correct contemplation that is without attainment.
"Emptiness" is an alternative name for the true mark of all phenomena, the dharma-nature, and the ultimate limit; it is not the emptiness perceived by the followers of the two vehicles.
This chapter is divided into three sections:
first, the announcement to the great assembly;

second, from "At that time, the Great King" onwards, the three rounds of question and answer in which Candraprabha makes his request, clarifying the meaning of protecting the fruit; [and third, the conclusion].
The third section, from "When the Buddha was preaching the Dharma" onwards, clarifies the benefits obtained by those present at the assembly.
Within the first part, the announcement, there are four sub-phrases;
the first is knowing the intentions of the sixteen kings.
1. "Second, 'I now descend' [indicates] the granting of permission to speak; 2.
'Listen attentively' [indicates] the command to listen; 3.
'At that time, King Prasenajit' [indicates] the offering of scattered flowers as worship."
At that time, the Buddha addressed the great assembly:

"Knowing that the sixteen great kings intend to inquire about the causes and conditions for protecting their kingdoms, I shall now first explain for the sake of all bodhisattvas the causes and conditions for protecting the fruit of Buddhahood and the causes and conditions for protecting the practices of the ten stages."
At that time, when the Buddha addressed the great assembly, he did so because he was about to deliver this teaching; such was the holy command.

As for the sixteen great kings who wished to inquire into the causes and conditions for protecting their kingdoms: it is the fundamental intention of these kings to ensure that the seven calamities do not arise and that malevolent disasters are extinguished, so that their territories may be peaceful and clear, and the myriad people may enjoy peace and happiness. This is the original purpose of the kings.
This introduces the scriptural passage on external protection, which is the "Chapter on Protecting the State" (*Rāṣṭrapālaparivarta*).
I shall first provide the following two points to clarify the permission for its exposition.
Now, one who wishes to guard both the internal and external must first establish their internal conduct.
When internal practice is perfected, external protection becomes complete; this is why internal protection is clarified first.
Regarding the protection of the Buddha-fruit, this refers to the scriptural text on protecting the fruit found in this chapter.
Regarding the protection of those who practice the ten stages, the following passage from the "Sūtra on Protecting the Causes" in the "Chapter on Teaching and Transforming" is presented:
"Listen attentively, listen attentively; reflect upon it well and practice in accordance with the Dharma."
At that time, King Prasenajit said:
"Excellent!
This is for the sake of a great causal connection."
He immediately scattered flowers of a billion kinds of colors, which transformed into a billion jeweled canopies that covered the great assembly.
From "Listen attentively" onwards, the Three Knowledges (trividyā) command the permission to speak.
When one intends to explain [the Dharma], first admonishing the assembly to listen attentively corresponds to the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*).
"Reflect upon it well" corresponds to the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*).
"Practice according to the Dharma" corresponds to the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*).
At that time, King Prasenajit descended and scattered flowers as an offering.
When the king said, "It is good," he was affirming what the Tathāgata had spoken; that which accords with principle and benefits sentient beings is called "good."

The "great causal condition" (mahābhisaṃbodhi-hetu-pratyaya) clearly explains the Prajñāpāramitā as the exhaustion of principles and the stillness of silence; this is precisely what the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* clarifies as the single great causal condition.
As for "scattering flowers," it intends to clarify devotion to the Dharma through the offering of scattered flowers.

That it transforms into a jeweled canopy illustrates that although the causes cultivated within the field of the Buddha may be small, the resulting fruits are vast; this is analogous to how small flowers can form a jeweled canopy.
The phrase "the great assembly" signifies that compassion universally covers all.
At that time, the Great King rose again, prostrated himself, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
"How do all Bodhisattvas protect the fruit of Buddhahood?
How do they protect the causal conditions for the practices of the ten stages?
At that time, the Great King rose again and paid homage; this concludes the second major section of the chapter, wherein Candraprabha inquires regarding the meaning of protecting the fruit.
Within this, there are three question-and-answer sections, which constitute three distinct parts:
the first question-and-answer clarifies that the two kinds of emptiness—of phenomena and of persons—are primordially quiescent and non-dual with the fruit of Buddhahood.
The second question asks: "Since sentient beings cannot be apprehended, how can they be transformed?
The answer is:
"If even causes and conditions are quiescent, how much more so are sentient beings?"
The third question concerns the emptiness of wisdom.
If wisdom were a substantial existence, its function of discernment and illumination could be distinguished;
since wisdom is already void and quiescent, how can its function of discernment and illumination be distinguished?
Answer:
Since even phenomena (dharma) are empty in their essence, how much more so is wisdom?
In the initial question-and-answer sequence, the question comes first and the answer follows.
Regarding the two lines within the inquiry:
first, "the moonlight is clear";
second, from "all bodhisattvas" onwards, the matters being requested are set forth.

Regarding the initial request, as for the Great King rising again to pay homage: since Candraprabha was the principal interlocutor for the profound mystery, he first manifested his reverent devotion before intending to pose his question.
Regarding the second matter requested, the first phrase requests protection for the fruit of Buddhahood, while the latter phrase requests protection for the practices of the ten stages (*bhūmi*).
The Buddha said:

"The Bodhisattva transforms the four modes of birth, yet does not contemplate the suchness of form, nor the suchness of sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; nor the suchness of sentient beings, self, person, permanence, bliss, selfhood, or purity; nor the suchness of the knower, the viewer, or the life-principle; nor the suchness of the Bodhisattva; nor the suchness of all practices, including the six perfections and the four means of attraction; nor the suchness of the two truths."
Regarding the Buddha’s response following the aforementioned question, the second part of the answer consists of two sections:
first, a general indication of the transformation of the four modes of birth;

second, from "not observing form" onwards, a detailed explanation according to various categories, showing that the two kinds of emptiness—of phenomena and of persons—are ungraspable, identical to the meaning of Suchness (*tathatā*), and non-dual and indistinguishable from the fruit of Buddhahood.
Question:

Since Candraprabha has requested an explanation of the causes and conditions for attaining the fruit of Buddhahood, the Buddha should have answered regarding the matter of that fruit; why then does he speak of transforming the four modes of birth?
Answer:
The various masters have spoken at length, which cannot be cited in full here.
Now it is said that this is intended to demonstrate the non-duality of cause and effect, clarifying that the ultimate emptiness of sentient beings is no different from that of the Buddha.
Therefore, the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra* states: "The suchness of sentient beings and the suchness of Maitreya are a single suchness, without duality.

For example, the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* says: "'Self' is the meaning of the Tathāgatagarbha. All phenomena discussed in this sutra, such as the four modes of birth, are entirely suchness, no different from the Buddha.
If one knows that the four modes of birth and the Buddha are non-dual and identical, this is precisely the protection of the fruit of Buddhahood.
How could such a dialogue be understood by worldly people?
Were it not for those who have long planted roots of goodness, encountered many Buddhas, and realized the emptiness of all phenomena, how else could they possibly correspond with this text?
Regarding what are called the four modes of birth: being born from a mother’s womb is therefore called "womb-birth" (jarāyu-ja);
Viśākhā’s mother giving birth to thirty-two eggs is called "egg-birth" (aṇḍa-ja);
and as with the courtesan Āmrapālī, it is called "moisture-birth" (saṃsveda-ja).
At the beginning of the kalpa, all beings were born by transformation.
Second, as explained below regarding the non-contemplation of form, there are two distinct sections clarifying the two kinds of emptiness—of birth and of phenomena. Regarding these two:
The first section extensively clarifies emptiness;
therefore, from "Thus, all... onwards is the second section, the summary.
Within the first section clarifying emptiness, there are four propositions:
First, it clarifies the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasunyatā*);
second, from "the assembly of sentient beings" onwards, it clarifies the emptiness of persons (*pudgalasunyatā*);
third, regarding the six perfections, it clarifies the emptiness of practice (*caryāsunyatā*).
In the section on the Fourfold Two Truths, it is clarified that both the objects and the teachings of the two truths are quiescent.
Regarding the initial phrase, "not contemplating form as such," there are numerous interpretations, which cannot be fully set forth here.

Now, according to the explanation in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, phenomena that arise from conditions are devoid of intrinsic nature by their very essence; they do not become non-existent only after being analyzed by wisdom.
This is intended to clarify that both the conditions and the contemplation are quiescent.
Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "Form itself cannot be apprehended, how much less that which is non-form.

Following the intent of this passage, one should fully clarify all four permutations; however, for the sake of brevity, it merely says "one does not contemplate form," and the same applies by analogy to feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
The Tripiṭaka Master said:
"If one were to eliminate form so as to return to suchness, one should say 'contemplating the suchness of form.
As for the text stating 'not contemplating the suchness of form,' this implies that if one eliminates form while retaining suchness, then the contemplation of the mind is not yet pure."
Now, in perfect contemplation (*yuan-guan*), one does not contemplate form, nor does one contemplate suchness; one does not perceive emptiness or existence, nor does one perceive object or wisdom.
All subsequent phrases are to be understood by this same principle.
Below the section on "sentient beings," the second part clarifies the emptiness of sentient beings (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) in seven statements:
because they arise within the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), they are called empty of sentient beings.
As for the "self" (*ātman*), it refers to the conceptualization of the five aggregates as a self.
"Person" is a provisional designation for the practitioner.
"Permanence, bliss, self, and purity" clarifies that the essence of sentient beings is empty.

Sentient beings are subject to inversion; they erroneously conceptualize within suffering, impermanence, non-self, and impurity what they take to be permanence, bliss, self, and purity. Therefore, it is said that birth and death are empty.

Now, it is said that the notions of "sentient beings," "self," and "person" are inverted dharmas, whereas the four virtues of permanence, bliss, self, and purity are pure dharmas. If one can realize that both of these are ultimately empty, this is therefore called "suchness."
Herein, it is intended to clarify that saṃsāra and nirvāṇa are non-dual.
"Suchness" (tathatā) is an alternative name for buddha-nature, dharma-nature, the right path, and non-duality.

Regarding "knowing and seeing" and "the life-span": mental consciousness is called "knowing," visual consciousness is called "seeing," and the non-interruption of the mind and form is called "the life-span.
As for "Bodhisattva," the mind of the Great Way is called a Bodhisattva.

Now, it is said that the preceding section clarified those who are transformed—the sentient beings—while this section distinguishes those who transform—the Bodhisattvas. Since both the agent and the object are pure, it is called "Suchness" (tathatā).
Third, the emptiness of practice is explained in three parts:

first, the six perfections; second, the four means of integration; and third, all dharmas of practice in their entirety. This clarifies that all these dharmas of Bodhisattva practice exist because they are Suchness.

The fourth section clarifies the suchness (*tathatā*) of the two truths: emptiness and existence constitute the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), while emptiness within existence constitutes the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). Therefore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "The suchness of the ultimate truth is the very suchness of the conventional truth."
The Buddha said, "So it is, so it is. This shall be explained separately in the later "Chapter on the Two Truths.

Therefore, the true nature of all phenomena is truly empty; they neither come nor go, are without arising or ceasing, are identical to the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), and equal to the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*). They are non-dual, undifferentiated, and like space. Thus, the aggregates, bases, and elements are without self and lack any marks of existence; this is the practice of the Bodhisattva’s transformation through the *prajñāpāramitā* of the ten stages.
Below this, the second section provides a summary answer to the previous question regarding the protection of the fruit and the protection of the cause.
This passage has two parts:

first, it concludes that the two kinds of emptiness regarding the dharmas of birth are identical to the equality of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), being non-dual and undifferentiated from the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*); it clarifies that the suchness of the four modes of birth is no different from the suchness of the Buddha, thereby elucidating the meaning of protecting the fruit.

This constitutes the answer to the question regarding the causal conditions for protecting the practices of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), following the section on the Bodhisattva’s transformative activity below the tenth stage; it clarifies that the meaning of "protecting" consists precisely in the Bodhisattva’s contemplative understanding.
First, the two types of emptiness regarding the dharmas of superior rebirth are established.
As for the phrase "the nature of all dharmas," it is another name for the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
"True emptiness" is not the emptiness understood by the followers of the Two Vehicles.
Coming from nowhere is called "not coming"; going nowhere is called "not going.
Although the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) has no coming or going, it nonetheless manifests as coming and going.
Regarding "neither arising nor ceasing": since phenomena are fundamentally unarisen, what cessation could there be?
"Identical to the true limit" means being identical to the *bhūtakoṭi* (actual limit) of all phenomena.
Regarding "equal to the dharma-nature," the *Śāstra* states: "Dharma is named *nirvāṇa*; nature is named the fundamental seed."
The term "etc. indicates that within all phenomena there is entirely the nature of peace and bliss (*sukha*).
This "nature of peace and bliss" is another name for *nirvāṇa*.
Regarding the phrase "without duality and without distinction," some say:
That there is no person outside of the Dharma is called "non-duality," and that there is no Dharma outside of persons is called "non-distinction.
Now, I say this is not so; it clarifies that the four modes of birth and the four virtues of permanence, bliss, self, and purity are non-dual and non-distinct.
That which is "like space" serves as a general metaphor for the non-existence of both persons and phenomena (*pudgala-dharma*).
Therefore, the statement that the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*) are without self (*anātman*) establishes the non-self of the person;
the statement that they are without any marks of existence establishes the non-self of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*).

This constitutes the "lower" section on Bodhisattvas, clarifying the Bodhisattva’s contemplative realization; it serves as a concluding response to the preceding inquiry regarding the causes for protection, demonstrating that because one awakens to non-attainment, one is able to realize the *prajñā* of the ten stages (*bhūmi*).
Therefore, the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā* states: "All are distinguished by means of the unconditioned dharma (*asaṃskṛtadharma*).
Seeing that both self and others are entirely unconditioned, one takes this very unconditioned state as the essence of a bodhisattva.
He addressed the Buddha, saying:
"If all phenomena are thus, does the bodhisattva protect and transform sentient beings for the sake of transforming those sentient beings?
This concludes the second question and answer following the address to the Buddha.
Candraprabha again requested an explanation of the previous meaning: "If sentient beings are ultimately unobtainable, how can they be transformed and brought to maturity?
This passage consists of two parts:
first, the question; second, the answer.
The question has three parts:
